title: Criminal Offending Among Persons with and without a Mental Illness: Does Employment, Housing, and Relationship Status Matter?
abstract: We used population data on persons born in Finland between 1980 and 1985 ( n = 391,174) to examine the risk of violent and property offending by age 35 among persons undiagnosed and diagnosed with a mental disorder (mood, psychotic, or alcohol) by age 25. We estimated population-averaged and fixed-effects models for associations between labor market status (employed, unemployed, disability pension) and living situation (married or cohabitating, living alone, not in a private dwelling) with offending for diagnosed and undiagnosed persons. Results indicated (a) unobserved individual differences accounted for a substantial portion of the associations between employment status and living situation with offending and (b) unemployment, living alone, and not living in a private dwelling were associated with a small risk of offending for those with and without a mental illness diagnosis in within-individual models. Results suggest life-course, bonding, and strain variables matter less than stable individual characteristics for offending risk.
